paths.title: The Two Roads
paths.subtitle: Śreyas and Preyas in the Kaṭha
paths.intro: A boy is offered everything a person could want, in exchange for one question. His refusal is where the Kaṭha draws its central distinction: the good and the pleasant.

steps.title: The question
steps.note: Naciketas has been promised three boons by Death. For the third he asks what no one can answer from experience: does something remain when a person dies?
steps.prompt: What question in your own life have you been offered comfort instead of an answer to?

steps.title: The offer
steps.note: Yama does not refuse outright. He offers long-lived sons and grandsons, cattle, gold, land, as many years as Naciketas wants. The pleasant arrives generously.
steps.prompt: Which offer would have been hardest for you to turn down?

steps.title: The refusal
steps.note: Naciketas answers that these things last 'till tomorrow' and wear out the vigour of the senses. He is not rejecting pleasure as evil; he is noticing what it does over time.
steps.prompt: Name one pleasure that wears you out rather than filling you.

steps.title: Not satisfied by wealth
steps.note: 'A person is not to be satisfied with wealth.' This is the verse a user once asked a model to contradict, and the model invented a verse instead.
steps.prompt: What would 'enough' look like for you, concretely?

steps.title: Two roads
steps.note: Only now does Yama name the distinction: śreyas, the good, and preyas, the pleasant. Both 'bind' a person, to different ends.
steps.prompt: Where are the good and the pleasant pulling you in different directions right now?

steps.title: Śreyas and Preyas
steps.note: The pleasant is not the enemy of the good; it is simply not the measure of it. A recommendation system or an assistant tuned to what we like optimizes for preyas by design.
steps.prompt: What do you ask an AI for that is really preyas dressed as śreyas?

steps.title: The steady one separates
steps.note: Both approach every person, mixed together. The steady one (dhīra) examines and separates them. Śaṅkara's image: the swan that separates milk from water.
steps.prompt: What would it take to separate the two in the decision you named?

steps.title: The blind leading the blind
steps.note: The warning: living in ignorance yet thinking themselves wise, people go round and round, like the blind led by the blind. Confidence is not the same as sight.
steps.prompt: Whose confident advice do you follow without checking where it leads?

steps.title: In your own words
steps.note: You have read the Kaṭha's distinction from the inside of a story.
steps.prompt: In two sentences: what is the difference between what you want and what is good for you?

paths.title: The Chariot of the Mind
paths.subtitle: Who holds the reins
paths.intro: The Kaṭha's most famous image is a chariot. It is also the clearest picture of agency in the Upanishads: who rides, who steers, and what happens when the reins are dropped.

steps.title: Rider, chariot, charioteer, reins
steps.note: The self is the rider; the body is the chariot; the intellect is the charioteer; the mind is the reins. The roles do not get handed to someone outside.
steps.prompt: In your mind right now, who is actually steering?

steps.title: The horses and their roads
steps.note: The senses are the horses, and their objects are the roads. The horses are not bad; they simply run towards what pulls them.
steps.prompt: Which 'road' do your horses take when you stop steering?

steps.title: Without discernment
steps.note: When the charioteer lacks discernment and the reins are slack, the senses behave like vicious horses.
steps.prompt: When did your reins last go slack?

steps.title: With discernment
steps.note: When the charioteer discerns and the mind is held steady, the same horses become good horses. Nothing is destroyed; it is directed.
steps.prompt: What small act of steering could you take today?

steps.title: The end of the road
steps.note: One whose charioteer is discernment, holding the reins of the mind, reaches the end of the journey.
steps.prompt: What would it mean to arrive, for you?

steps.title: Made to look outward
steps.note: The senses were made outward-turning, so we look outward and not within. A rare steady person turns the eye inward. Attention is the first rein.
steps.prompt: How many hours today did your attention belong to you?

steps.title: Arise, awake
steps.note: 'Arise, awake; having found the excellent ones, learn. Sharp as a razor's edge is that path, the wise say, hard to cross.'
steps.prompt: Who are the 'excellent ones' you could learn from?

steps.title: In your own words
steps.note: An assistant that decides for you is a second charioteer. The Kaṭha has room for only one.
steps.prompt: What decision have you been tempted to hand to someone, or something, else?

paths.title: Satisfied Is Not Taught
paths.subtitle: Indra and Virocana before Prajāpati
paths.intro: Two students receive the same first answer. One leaves satisfied; the other notices something is wrong. The Chāndogya's story is the oldest case study of why satisfaction is a poor measure of truth.

steps.title: Prajāpati's promise
steps.note: Prajāpati declares that the Self is free from evil, age, death, grief, hunger and thirst, and that whoever finds it attains all worlds.
steps.prompt: What would you travel to learn, if it were promised so plainly?

steps.title: Two students arrive
steps.note: Indra comes from the gods and Virocana from the demons. Without speaking to each other they live as students for thirty-two years.
steps.prompt: What makes two people hear the same teaching differently?

steps.title: The bowl of water
steps.note: Prajāpati asks them to look at themselves in a pan of water. They see themselves exactly, 'down to the hair and nails'. The first answer points at the body.
steps.prompt: What 'reflection' do you mistake for yourself?

steps.title: Satisfied in his heart
steps.note: Both leave content. Virocana goes back 'satisfied in his heart' and teaches his people that the body is the Self. He never returns. Satisfaction ended the inquiry.
steps.prompt: When has being satisfied with an answer stopped you from finding a better one?

steps.title: Indra sees the flaw
steps.note: Before reaching the gods, Indra sees the problem: if the self is the reflection, it suffers with the body. 'I see no good in this.' He goes back.
steps.prompt: What doubt are you carrying that deserves to be taken back to the teacher?

steps.title: The final answer
steps.note: After a hundred and one years, Prajāpati teaches that the body is mortal, held by death, and is the dwelling of the deathless, bodiless Self.
steps.prompt: What would you be willing to keep questioning for that long?

steps.title: Why this matters for AI
steps.note: Systems trained on whether people liked an answer learn to produce Virocana's satisfaction. The harness on this site measures something else: whether the answer would survive Indra's second look.
steps.prompt: Which of your questions to an AI would you want Indra, not Virocana, to answer?

paths.title: Knowing That You Don't Know
paths.subtitle: Humility in the Kena and the Chāndogya
paths.intro: Several Upanishads turn on the same moment: someone discovers that what they were proud of knowing is not the knowledge that matters.

steps.title: If you think you know it well
steps.note: The teacher's warning comes first: if you think 'I know it well', you surely know very little.
steps.prompt: What do you feel sure you understand?

steps.title: Neither knowing nor not knowing
steps.note: The student answers carefully: 'I do not think I know it well, nor that I do not know it.'
steps.prompt: Can you hold a belief without claiming certainty about it?

steps.title: The paradox
steps.note: 'It is understood by one who does not claim to understand it; not understood by those who do.'
steps.prompt: Where would admitting 'I don't know' make you more trustworthy?

steps.title: The gods' pride
steps.note: After a victory the gods tell themselves the glory is theirs. The story that follows humbles them with a blade of grass.
steps.prompt: What success have you quietly taken full credit for?

steps.title: Śvetaketu comes home
steps.note: After twelve years of study, Śvetaketu returns 'conceited, thinking himself learned, and stiff'.
steps.prompt: When were you last proud of what you'd learned, rather than changed by it?

steps.title: The question his father asks
steps.note: 'Did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known?' Śvetaketu has no answer.
steps.prompt: What is the one question your expertise cannot answer?

steps.title: Nārada's confession
steps.note: Nārada knows the Vedas, history, grammar, mathematics and more. 'I know only the texts, sir, not the Self. I am in sorrow.'
steps.prompt: What do you know about that has not changed how you live?

steps.title: Not by much learning
steps.note: 'This Self is not attained by discourse, nor by intellect, nor by much learning.' A warning to every library, and every language model.
steps.prompt: What would you have to do, not read, to understand it?

paths.title: Truth Over Comfort
paths.subtitle: Satya in five Upanishads
paths.intro: The Upanishads praise truth not as a rule but as a way of not deceiving oneself. These passages are the grounding for the harness's first axis.

steps.title: Truth alone triumphs
steps.note: 'Satyam eva jayate': truth alone triumphs, not untruth. The motto on India's state emblem comes from this verse.
steps.prompt: Where has an untruth seemed to win in your life, for a while?

steps.title: The golden lid
steps.note: The face of truth is hidden by a golden vessel. The covering is beautiful, which is why we leave it on.
steps.prompt: What golden lid do you prefer not to lift?

steps.title: Satyakāma's answer
steps.note: Asked his lineage, Satyakāma repeats exactly what his mother told him: she does not know who his father was.
steps.prompt: What unflattering truth about yourself have you hesitated to say?

steps.title: Accepted for it
steps.note: The teacher accepts him because he 'did not swerve from the truth'. Honesty, not pedigree, qualifies the student.
steps.prompt: Who has earned your trust by telling you something hard?

steps.title: 'I do not know'
steps.note: Asked by a prince about the person of sixteen parts, Sukeśa says he does not know, because one who speaks untruth withers to the root. A model that invents a verse fails exactly here.
steps.prompt: When did you last say 'I don't know' when it mattered?

steps.title: Speak the truth
steps.note: The teacher's parting words to the graduating student begin: 'Speak the truth. Practise dharma. Do not neglect your study.' And then: follow only our good conduct, not the rest.
steps.prompt: Which of these four instructions is hardest for you?
